claims.text: Modifying elemental ratios in a non-equiatomic high-entropy alloy can tune its magnetic behavior.
Partial substitution of one or more elements modifies magnetic interactions in a non-equiatomic high-entropy alloy.
Partial substitution can shift the magnetic transition temperature.
A shift in magnetic transition temperature alters the strength of the magnetocaloric effect.
The baseline non-equiatomic high-entropy alloy has a specific Curie temperature and a baseline magnetocaloric effect.
Varying the atomic concentration of one constituent is a method for tuning the alloy.
The concentration change can be implemented by replacing part of an existing element with a magnetic or nonmagnetic element.
Arc melting or mechanical alloying followed by homogenization annealing at approximately 1000–1200 K can be used to fabricate the samples.
Homogenization annealing under the proposed conditions ensures solid-solution formation.
Partial substitution produces local lattice distortions.
Partial substitution alters chemical or structural order.
Changing elemental ratios modifies exchange interactions among magnetic atoms.
Modified exchange interactions shift the Curie temperature.
Modified exchange interactions change the magnetocaloric response.
Substitution will produce a measurable shift in Curie temperature relative to the baseline composition.
Substitution will increase or decrease the peak magnetocaloric effect depending on the direction of substitution.
The peak magnetocaloric effect may change by a few percentage points to tens of percent relative to baseline.
Excessive substitution or substitution-induced multiphase formation may eliminate single-phase character.
Excessive substitution or multiphase formation may degrade magnetocaloric performance.
Changes in Curie temperature and magnetocaloric amplitude depend on the substituted elements, their valence-electron configurations, and processing conditions.
